title: Galaxy cluster MACS J1720+35
caption: The galaxy cluster MACSJ1720+35, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble image shows the heart of a vast galaxy cluster called MACSJ1720+35, seen in visible and near-infrared light. In the top right, just barely visible, is an exploding star nicknamed Caracalla, which lies behind the cluster.

The cluster's mass is so great that its gravity warps, brightens and enlarges the light of objects behind it, an effect called gravitational lensing. Caracalla is a Type Ia supernova, a kind of stellar explosion that astronomers value because it reaches a consistent peak brightness, which makes it useful for estimating distances.

Because astronomers know how bright a Type Ia supernova should be, a lensed one lets them check how strongly the cluster is magnifying things, testing the optical prescription of the cluster lens. Caracalla was one of three exploding stars found in the CLASH survey with Hubble.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and Advanced Camera for Surveys, using filters from visible light into the near-infrared. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the faint supernova behind the cluster needed Hubble's long exposures to show up at all.

explore: CLASH, the Cluster Lensing And Supernova survey with Hubble, charted how dark matter is spread through 25 galaxy clusters. Dark matter is invisible, yet it is believed to account for most of the matter in the Universe.
Follow-up observations of Caracalla came from a Hubble program run by the Supernova Cosmology Project.
